Chapter 8: The Challenge of Generosity—Letting Go of More.
Have you ever noticed how money seems to shine a spotlight on what really matters to us? For some, it’s a constant source of stress. For others, it’s a way to keep score, or maybe even a safety net against the unknown.
So when the idea of giving comes up—especially giving when it actually costs you something—it can feel risky. Maybe even a little bit crazy.
But here’s the thing: generosity isn’t about how much you have. It’s about the heart behind what you give.
Let me tell you about a couple who were just scraping by. They heard about a family in their neighborhood who’d lost everything in a fire. Now, they didn’t have a lot—certainly not extra. But they still offered up a spare room, shared meals, and even gathered a few friends to help. It wasn’t all smooth sailing. There were days when they worried if they’d stretched themselves too thin, moments when they second-guessed their decision.
But as they watched this family slowly rebuild, something unexpected happened. Their own lives started to feel richer, not poorer.
See, a lot of us think generosity is just for the wealthy. You know, folks with plenty to spare. But some of the most powerful acts of giving actually come from people who don’t have much at all.
It’s not about writing a huge check or making a splashy donation. It’s about being willing to let go—trusting that there really is enough to go around.
There’s a story of a young professional who started to realize how tightly he clung to his stuff. The higher he climbed at work, the more he worried about losing what he’d earned. So, he tried something new. He gave to causes he cared about, helped out friends, and started picking experiences over more things.
The fear didn’t vanish overnight, but it slowly started to fade. In fact, he found a new kind of freedom in giving—a sense that he was part of something bigger than just himself.
Generosity isn’t just about money, though. It’s your time, your attention, your presence. Sometimes, it’s simply sharing what you have—even when it feels like it’s not quite enough.
Most of us worry about running out, don’t we? But here’s the beautiful paradox: the more you give, the more you tend to receive. Not always in dollars, but in joy, in connection, and in a sense of meaning.
Think about the retired nurse who, living on a fixed income, spent her afternoons visiting homebound neighbors, delivering meals and sharing stories. What she had to offer wasn’t money—but her time, her kindness, and her prayers made all the difference. For the people she visited, she was a bright spot in their day.
And for her, giving her time felt just as valuable as any financial gift.
Here’s something to remember: the challenge of generosity never really goes away. There will always be reasons to hold back, to play it safe.
But those who dare to let go often discover that life actually gets fuller, not emptier. Generosity isn’t about losing—it’s about making space for abundance.
Most of us don’t realize how much we have to give... until we start giving.
So, here’s the invitation: open your hands, trust that there’s enough, and find the joy that comes from living generously.
